amendments.rule: A repeated or resumptive element that the ASV renders once is still its own unit. Mark the unrepresented occurrence `unrepresented` rather than folding it into the rendered one. Where the repetition is a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral — Hebrew writes one `שָׁנָה` per numeral group where the ASV writes a single *years* — the rendered occurrence is the last, closing the whole Hebrew figure as the English noun closes the whole English one. Do not settle it by number agreement: Hebrew writes `שָׁנִים` after 2–10 and `שָׁנָה` from 11 up whatever the total, while the English plural follows the sum, so a match between them is an accident of two unrelated agreement systems and is not evidence. Do not settle it by which numeral the English noun stands beside either, since English drives the counted noun to the end of the phrase whatever order the translation chose. Tail-to-tail is what survives, and it holds across both Hebrew group orders and the ASV's frequent reordering of them. The genealogies are where this recurs, and BSB, which attaches the noun to its own phrase, disagrees on every first occurrence. **Tail-to-tail governs a run of absolute occurrences only.** Where the phrase is instead headed by a **construct** — a regnal date such as `בִּשְׁנַת עֶשְׂרִים וָשֶׁבַע שָׁנָה` → *In the twenty and seventh year* — the construct is what the English realizes, and the trailing absolute is the resumptive occurrence that goes `unrepresented`. So the rendered occurrence is the last of several absolutes but the first where a construct heads them, and MACULA's morphology is what decides which case this is. Position is the consequence, not the rule. **But a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a fused English word is not an unrendered occurrence.** Where a relative clause resumes its antecedent with a pronominal suffix on a preposition, or with a resumptive adverb, and the ASV writes one pronominal adverb for the whole — *wherein*, *whereon*, *whereby*, *whither*, and the bare *therein* of a preposition and its own suffix — the relative, the preposition and the resumptive morpheme share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative, or on the preposition where no relative stands. Do not mark the suffix `unrepresented` under this rule's first sentence: rule 30's one-English-word condition is met, because that word carries the resumption as well as the relation, exactly as *Nor* carries both the coordination and the negation in rule 35. The corpus reads `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ` → *wherein* as one three-morpheme unit in twenty-one places and `בָּהּ` → *therein* as one two-morpheme unit in sixty-one, and records no unit where such a suffix stands outside the word. So ask first whether the English word carries the morpheme's sense: what this rule's first sentence governs is an element the ASV has left unwritten, as a second `בֵּין` or a surplus `שָׁנָה` is, and not one it has written inside a fusion. **A resumptive possessive suffix is read on exactly those terms, and it need not stand on a preposition.** Where the clause resumes its antecedent with a suffix on a noun inside it and the ASV writes one *whose* for the pair, the relative and that suffix share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative, while the noun keeps its own English: `אֶרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אֲבָנֶיהָ בַרְזֶל` → *a land* ***whose*** *stones are iron* is one unit on `אֲשֶׁר` and the suffix, with *stones* left to `אֶבֶן`. Contiguity is not the condition, for the reason rule 35 gives: however much of the clause stands between them, the one English word still carries both the relation and the resumption, so nothing is left over to mark. The corpus reads `אֲשֶׁר` with its resumptive suffix as one *whose* unit at DEU.28.49 and 1KI.8.39, and as a `noncompositional` one at AMO.2.9 and DAN.10.1 among eighteen such places. **But read which morphemes stand in each clause before counting a second occurrence.** Where a further clause is coordinated under the one written relative and the ASV rewrites its *whose* at the head of that clause, a resumptive suffix standing in that clause is what the second word realizes, under rule 18's sentence giving a suffix the English relative pronoun that renders it: `וּמֵהֲרָרֶיהָ תַּחְצֹב נְחֹשֶׁת` → *and out of* ***whose*** *hills thou mayest dig copper* gives its *whose* to the suffix on `הֲרָרֶיהָ`, not to the relative as a repetition under rule 25. Where no such suffix stands in the coordinated clause, rule 55's distributed subordinator governs as before and every occurrence is the relative's. **And read whether the suffix points at the antecedent at all before treating it as resumptive.** Every fusion above rests on a morpheme that resumes the antecedent, and a pronominal suffix standing inside the relative clause does that only where its referent is the antecedent; agreement is the first check and reference decides, so read MACULA's person, gender and number against the noun the clause modifies. Where the suffix instead denotes something else the clause speaks of, the one English pronominal adverb carries the relative's own relation and nothing of that suffix, rule 30's condition is unmet for it, and the fusion does not reach it: the relative takes the adverb alone, the suffix takes whatever English pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and the preposition it stands on is disposed of by rules 11 and 40 like any other. `וְאֶת־תַּחֲלֻאֶיהָ אֲשֶׁר־חִלָּה יְהוָה בָּהּ` → *and the sicknesses* ***wherewith*** *Jehovah hath made* ***it*** *sick* gives *wherewith* to `אֲשֶׁר` alone, *it* to the suffix of `בָּהּ`, which is feminine singular and denotes the land rather than the masculine plural `תַּחֲלֻאִים` the relative modifies, and leaves the `בְּ` `unrepresented` under rule 40, since the ASV promotes its object to the direct object of *made ... sick*. A relative left holding such a word by itself is not a unit short of its parts: the corpus aligns a bare `אֲשֶׁר` to *wherewith* in fifty-five units, and its *wherein* units include bare relatives beside the three-morpheme fusions. Count the English pronouns against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s: where the ASV writes a pronoun besides the adverb, some morpheme other than the relative answers for it, and where it writes none, the resumption is inside the adverb and the paragraphs above govern.
amendments.why: DEU.29.22 had to correct itself inside the verse. The first analysis fused אֲשֶׁר + בְּ + הּ of `אֲשֶׁר־חִלָּה יְהוָה בָּהּ` into *wherewith* under this rule and then handed the *it* of *made it sick* to the possessive suffix on תַּחֲלֻאֶיהָ, which the ASV renders by nothing. That is wrong on the Hebrew: בָּהּ is 3fs and its referent is the land, while the antecedent תַּחֲלֻאִים is masculine plural, so the suffix never resumed the antecedent and the single English word never carried its sense. Rule 22's fusion paragraphs say 'resumes its antecedent' twice but give no test for whether it does, and they close with the corpus observation that no such suffix stands outside the word — which reads, to a pass meeting this shape, as an instruction to fuse whatever suffix is in the clause. The amendment adds the agreement-and-reference test and says where the pieces go when it fails, so the next chapter meeting a non-resumptive suffix inside a relative clause does not reproduce the error. The corpus in front of me carries it: `אֲשֶׁר` is aligned to *wherewith* on its own in fifty-five units, and the *wherein* group holds bare relatives (1KI.2.26) alongside the `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ` fusions, so both shapes are already attested and nothing here contradicts the counts the rule already cites. Everything else in rule 22 — the counted-noun tail-to-tail reasoning, the construct exception, both fusion paragraphs and the coordinated-clause carve-out — is returned unchanged.

conventions: The Hebrew positive existential יֵשׁ is read on the terms rule 50 gives the Aramaic אִיתַי. It takes whatever overt finite frame the ASV writes, the supplied dummy subject included, headed on the copular verb rather than on the *there*: פֶּן יֵשׁ בָּכֶם אִישׁ → *lest* ***there should be*** *among you man* (DEU.29.18, twice). Where the clause writes a predicate of its own and the ASV spends no separate frame on the particle, it is `unrepresented`, and a suffix on it goes the same way under rule 22 where the relative's supplied antecedent already carries the reference: אֲשֶׁר יֶשְׁנוֹ פֹּה עִמָּנוּ עֹמֵד → *him that standeth here with us* leaves both יֵשׁ and its suffix nothing, while the אַיִן of the answering clause takes *is not* under rule 50 because no participle stands there to hold the copula.

Where the ASV writes a lexically contentful English verb in the slot a copula would occupy in a verbless clause, this chapter joins that verb to the predicate morpheme rather than marking it `added`: מֶה חֳרִי הָאַף הַגָּדוֹל הַזֶּה → ***what meaneth*** *the heat of this great anger* gives *what meaneth* to מָה, which is the clause's predicate, on the reasoning rule 49 uses for a belonging verb written where a copula would stand and rule 20 uses for מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה → *What man* ***is*** *this*. The same chapter reads לַיהוָה → *belong unto Jehovah* and לָנוּ → *belong unto us* that way at DEU.29.29, and יֹאבֶה → *will* at DEU.29.20, where dropping the word leaves that verb with no rendering at all. The competing reading treats *meaneth* as rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb and marks it `added`, leaving מָה the bare *what*; it is recorded at DEU.29.24 and was not taken, since only the clause's predication and not מָה's own sense is lost when the word is dropped.

report: Read all 53 candidate groups and then the dump verse by verse, since the table is keyed by source lemma and this chapter carries seven `added` units it cannot see. No construction is analysed two ways without the source or the ASV licensing the difference, so patches is empty.

Compound prepositions are uniform: מֵעַל (29.5 twice, 29.28), מֵעִם (29.18) and מֵאַחֲרֵי (29.22) are each one fused unit headed on מִן, and the source head does not move when the ASV writes *of* at 29.28 where it wrote *upon* at 29.5. That is the trap rule 23 names, correctly avoided.

בָּהּ is read two ways and both are right: fused to *therein* at 29.23, split at 29.22 with בְּ `unrepresented` and the suffix taking *it*, because *it* carries only the pronoun while *therein* carries both morphemes (rules 30, 40). Likewise וְ+לֹא splits at 29.4, where two English words are written, and fuses at 29.6, 29.14 and 29.23 twice, where one is; the 29.6 fusion is rule 35's across a fronted object.

יֵשׁ takes the ASV's frame at 29.18 twice and is `unrepresented` at 29.15, where עֹמֵד is the clause's own predicate. That difference is licensed, and it is logged as a convention because rule 50 states the reading only for the Aramaic אִיתַי. אֵת H853 takes English at 29.9 alone (*prosper in*, rule 16's first family) and is `unrepresented` in its other occurrences.

Article counting runs per phrase throughout and agrees with itself: a written *the* goes to an article standing before its own word, and the article is `unrepresented` wherever a demonstrative pronoun or a supplied construct determiner holds the phrase's one determiner. The construct chains with articled recta (29.1, 7, 8, 9, 16, 19, 21, 22, 24, 29) all divide by rule 29's arthrous/anarthrous test, with nothing fronted where the rectum's own word carries a determiner.

All seven `added` units were checked against the morphemes standing in their own clauses — 29.10 *even* (no marker there; the clause's waw already holds its *and*), 29.15 *also* (rule 51), 29.23's four italicised connectives (no conjunction in those clauses), 29.25 *men* (rule 17). No comparable supplied word elsewhere in the chapter was folded into a neighbour instead, so the count is symmetric.

BSB: 50 disagreements, none a genuine error. Td × 32, R × 6 and To × 4 are the documented convention difference. Every named singleton is a place the ASV writes nothing at all: the apodosis waw at 29.7, the paragogic nun at 29.9, the second suffix of אִתְּכֶם לְבַדְּכֶם at 29.14, יֶשְׁנוֹ and both existential suffixes at 29.15, the possessive on תַּחֲלֻאֶיהָ at 29.22, the object suffix of יְדָעוּם at 29.26.

One live tie is left standing: 29.24 מֶה → *what meaneth*. The verse names the competing reading, in which *meaneth* is rule 20's supplied lexical verb and therefore `added`. I did not re-decide it; it is recorded as a convention so a later reader finds the argument rather than the edge alone.

One amendment, to rule 22. DEU.29.22 corrected itself inside the verse: the first analysis fused אֲשֶׁר + בְּ + הּ into *wherewith* and gave the *it* to the possessive on תַּחֲלֻאֶיהָ. בָּהּ is 3fs and denotes the land, not the masculine plural antecedent, so it resumes nothing. Rule 22's fusion paragraphs say 'resumes its antecedent' but give no test for it, so the next pass would make the same mistake; the amendment supplies the test and the disposal.
